      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Juvenile</span> Rheumatoid <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span></content>

      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Childhood</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">JRA</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Juvenile</span> idiopathic <span class="qt0">arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> (JA) is <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that happens in <span class="qt1">children</span>. It causes joint inflammation (swelling), pain, stiffness, and loss of motion. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee. It can affect any joint, but it is more common in the knees, hands, and feet.</p><p>JA can affect your child's growth and development, and in some cases, it can also affect other organs. Finding JA early and starting treatment can help manage symptoms and reduce joint damage.</p>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt1">juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>There are several other forms of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> affecting <span class="qt1">children</span>. The most common type of JA in <span class="qt1">children</span> under age 16 is <span class="qt1">juvenile</span> idiopathic <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> (JIA). There are multiple types of JIA. Symptoms and the number of joints affected help determine the type. Some types of JIA are more common in girls.</p>What causes <span class="qt1">juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>The exact cause of JA is unknown. Most types are autoimmune disorders. This means that your immune system, which normally helps your body fight infection, attacks your body's tissues.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1">juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Symptoms can vary depending on the type of JA. The symptoms of most types include joint pain, swelling, warmth, and stiffness. Your child may not complain of pain or stiffness, but one early sign of JA may be limping or clumsiness in the morning or after resting. Larger joints, such as the knee, may be swollen.</p><p>Certain types of JA can cause a high fever, swollen lymph nodes, a rash, growth problems, or eye inflammation in some <span class="qt1">children</span>. Symptoms can come and go. Some <span class="qt1">children</span> have just one or two flare-ups. Others have symptoms that never go away.</p>How is <span class="qt1">juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> diagnosed?<p>There is no single test for JA, so it can be hard to diagnose. Your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about medical history and symptoms.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging studies.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>A team of providers usually treats JA. Treatment will depend on your child's age, the type of JA, and how bad it is. Treatment can include medicines and physical therapy to help maintain movement and reduce swelling and pain.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span> and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/arthritis.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Joint inflammation</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee.</p><p>Most types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> you have.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Common types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Osteoarthritis</span> is the most common type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. It's often related to aging or injury.</li><li>Autoimmune <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake.  Rheumatoid <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is the most common form of this type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>.</li><li><span class="qt1">Juvenile</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is a type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that happens in <span class="qt1">children</span>.</li><li>Infectious <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is one type.</li><li>Psoriatic <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> affects people with psoriasis (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches).</li><li>Gout is a painful type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected.</li><li>Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever, weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash.</p><p>Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> may be signs of other illnesses.</p>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>A few things that might increase your chance of getting <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include:</p><ul><li>Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> if a member of your family has the disorder.</li><li>Age. The risk of getting many types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> increases with age.</li><li>Sex. Certain types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> are more common in women, while other types are more common in men.</li></ul><p>Other factors that might increase your risk of getting <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include having a previous joint injury, obesity, or lupus.</p>How is <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask you about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or take x-rays.</li></ul><p>Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> care) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Treatment depends on the type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> you have. It may include medicine or surgery. Your provider will work with you to improve your symptoms and quality of life.</p><p>A few ways to help manage your symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Hot or cold packs</li><li>Relaxation techniques</li><li>Use of splints, braces, and/or assistive devices</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span> and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/eyediseases.html">
      <content name="title">Eye Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ophthalmology</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Pinguecula</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What diseases can affect the eye?<p>Even if your eyes feel healthy, you could have a problem and not know it. That's why regular eye exams are so important. Refractive errors are the most common type of vision problem that makes it hard to see clearly. But some eye conditions or diseases don't have any symptoms and can lead to a permanent loss of vision.</p><p>Some common eye diseases and conditions include:</p><ul><li>Cataracts, which happens when the clear lens in the front of your eye becomes cloudy. Cataracts are common as you get older and can lead to vision loss.</li><li>Optic nerve disorders, which includes glaucoma. Glaucoma usually happens when the fluid pressure inside your eyes slowly rises.</li><li>Retinal disorders, which are problems with the nerve layer at the back of your eye.</li><li>Macular degeneration, which is a disease that destroys your sharp, central vision.</li><li>Diabetic eye problems, which can cause vision loss and blindness.</li><li>Conjunctivitis, which is an infection also known as pink eye. It can cause pink or red itchy eyes. Some types of pink eye can spread very easily.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of eye diseases?<p>Some eye conditions and diseases do not always have symptoms. Early detection through a comprehensive dilated eye exam could help your eye care provider detect diseases in the early stages. Proper treatment could help slow or prevent vision loss.</p><p>Get regular eye exams and call your eye care professional right away if you notice any of these symptoms:</p><ul><li>A sudden change in vision</li><li>Everything looks dim</li><li>Flashes of light</li><li>Eye pain</li><li>Double vision</li><li>Fluid coming from your eye</li><li>Inflammation (swelling)</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop eye diseases?<p>Getting older increases your risk of some eye diseases. Other things that may put you at a higher risk of some eye diseases can include if you:</p><ul><li>Are overweight or obese</li><li>Have a family history of eye disease</li><li>Are African American, Hispanic, or Native American</li><li>Have certain health conditions such as Diabetic eye problems, or high blood pressure</li></ul>What are the treatments for eye diseases?<p>Treatment may depend on the eye condition or disease but can include:</p><ul><li>A new prescription for eyeglasses or contacts</li><li>Use of bright lights or magnifying lenses for reading and other activities</li><li>Medicines</li><li>Prescription eye drops or ointments</li><li>Laser treatment</li><li>Surgery</li></ul><p>Depending on your eye condition or disease, treatment may slow vision loss but may not restore vision. Talk to your provider about what treatment is best for you.</p>Can eye diseases be prevented?<p>Your best defense is to have regular checkups. Be sure to tell your provider if any eye diseases run in your family.</p><p>You can also help take care of your vision by making lifestyle changes to lower your risk of health conditions that can cause vision problems. This could include by:</p><ul><li>Protecting your eyes from the sun</li><li>Wearing protective eyewear while using tools or playing certain sports</li><li>Getting regular physical activity</li><li>Staying at a healthy weight</li><li>Quitting smoking (or not starting)</li><li>Eating a healthy diet</li></ul><p>NIH: National Eye Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/myositis.html">
      <content name="title">Myositis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dermatomyositis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Polymyositis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Myositis means inflammation of the muscles that you use to move your body. An injury, infection, or autoimmune disease can cause it. Two specific kinds are polymyositis and dermatomyositis. Polymyositis causes muscle weakness, usually in the muscles closest to the trunk of your body. Dermatomyositis causes muscle weakness, plus a skin rash.</p><p>Other symptoms of myositis may include:</p><ul><li>Fatigue after walking or standing</li><li>Tripping or falling</li><li>Trouble swallowing or breathing</li></ul><p>Doctors may use a physical exam, lab tests, imaging tests and a muscle biopsy to diagnose myositis. There is no cure for these diseases, but you can treat the symptoms. Polymyositis and dermatomyositis are first treated with high doses of a corticosteroid. Other options include medications, physical therapy, exercise, heat therapy, assistive devices, and rest.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/osteoporosis.html">
      <content name="title">Osteoporosis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Bone Loss</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is osteoporosis?<p>Osteoporosis is a disease in which your bones become weak and are likely to fracture (break). The disease can develop when your bone mineral density and bone mass decrease. It can also happen if the structure and strength of your bones change.</p><p>Osteoporosis is called a "silent" disease because it doesn't usually cause symptoms. You may not even know you have the disease until you break a bone. This could happen with any bone, but it's most common in the bones of your hip, vertebrae in the spine, and wrist.</p>What causes osteoporosis?<p>Your bones are made of living tissue. To keep them strong, your body breaks down old bone and replaces it with new bone. Osteoporosis develops when more bone is broken down than replaced. You lose bone mass and changes happen in the structure of your bone tissue. This can happen as you get older. Other risk factors can also lead to the development of osteoporosis or increase your chance of developing the disease.</p>Who is more likely to develop osteoporosis?<p>Anyone can develop osteoporosis, but you are more likely to develop it if you have one or more risk factors:</p><ul><li>Your sex. Osteoporosis is more common in women, especially after menopause (postmenopausal).</li><li>Your age. Your risk increases as you get older. It is most common in people over age 50.</li><li>Your body size. It is more common in people who are slim and thin boned.</li><li>Your race:<ul><li>White and Asian women are at highest risk.</li><li>African American and Mexican American women have a lower risk.</li><li>White men are at higher risk than African American and Mexican American men.</li></ul></li><li>Family history. Your risk of osteoporosis may be higher if one of your parents has osteoporosis or broke their hip.</li><li>Changes to hormones. Low levels of certain hormones can increase your chance of developing osteoporosis.</li><li>Diet. A diet that is low in calcium and/or vitamin D or does not include enough protein can raise your risk.</li><li>Long-term use of certain medicines, such as:
	<ul><li>Corticosteroids</li><li>Proton pump inhibitors (which treat GERD)</li><li>Medicines to treat epilepsy</li></ul>
</li><li>Having other medical conditions, such as:
	<ul><li>Endocrine diseases</li><li>Certain digestive diseases</li><li>Rheumatoid <span class="qt0">arthritis</span></li><li>Certain types of cancer</li><li>HIV</li><li>Anorexia nervosa, a type of eating disorder</li></ul>
</li><li>Your lifestyle. Certain lifestyle factors can contribute to bone loss, such as:
	<ul><li>Smoking tobacco</li><li>Long-term heavy alcohol use</li><li>Physical inactivity or prolonged periods of bedrest</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the symptoms of osteoporosis?<p>Osteoporosis usually doesn't cause symptoms. You may not know that you have it until you break a bone.</p>How is osteoporosis diagnosed?<p>Health care providers often diagnose osteoporosis during routine screening for the disease. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for:</p><ul><li>Women age 65 and older</li><li>Postmenopausal women under age 65 who have factors that increase the chance of developing osteoporosis</li></ul><p>For men, it isn't clear yet whether regular screening is helpful. More research is needed to know for sure.</p><p>To find out if you have osteoporosis, your provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history and whether you have ever broken a bone</li><li>May do a physical exam, which could include checking for:
	<ul><li>A loss of height and/or weight</li><li>Changes in your posture</li><li>Balance and gait (the way you walk)</li><li>Your muscle strength</li></ul>
</li><li>Will likely order a bone density scan</li><li>May do a fracture risk assessment, which is a short questionnaire that helps estimate your risk of breaking a bone in the next 10 years
</li><li>Will likely order a bone density scan</li><li>May do a fracture risk assessment, which is a short questionnaire that helps estimate your risk of breaking a bone in the next 10 years</li></ul>What are the treatments for osteoporosis?<p>The goals for treating osteoporosis are to slow or stop bone loss and to prevent fractures. Your provider may recommend:</p><ul><li>A healthy, balanced diet that includes enough calcium, vitamin D, and protein</li><li>Lifestyle changes such as quitting smoking and limiting alcohol</li><li>Regular physical activity including weight-bearing exercise (like walking), strength training, and balance exercises</li><li>Fall prevention to help prevent fractures</li><li>Medicines, such as:
	<ul><li>Medicines that slow down bone loss</li><li>Medicines that help rebuild bone</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>In addition to managing your osteoporosis, it's important to avoid activities that may cause a fracture. These can include movements that involve:</p><ul><li>Twisting your spine, like swinging a golf club</li><li>Bending forward from the waist, like sit ups and toe touches</li></ul><p>You can also help reduce the risk of breaking a bone by preventing falls.</p>Can osteoporosis be prevented?<p>To help keep bones strong and help prevent osteoporosis, the best thing to do is to eat a healthy diet rich in calcium and vitamin D. Getting regular physical activity, limiting alcohol, and not smoking can also help.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span> and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>
